q: 66. The soil involved in the compaction is .............
explain: Compaction is a mechanical process applied to partly saturated (moist, unsaturated) soil to expel air from voids.

q: 67. The maximum compaction for any given water content corresponds to a per cent air-voids equal to .............
explain: Maximum theoretical compaction (the zero air voids line) corresponds to 0% air voids for a given water content.

q: 68. In the modified proctor test the drop height of the rammer is .............
explain: The Modified Proctor test uses a heavier rammer dropped from 45 cm, giving higher compactive effort than the Standard Proctor test.

q: 69. The admixture used in soil stabilization is .............
explain: Cement, lime, and bitumen are all commonly used admixtures for soil stabilization, depending on soil type and application.

q: 70. The bearing capacity of a soil does not depend on .............
explain: Bearing capacity is a soil/footing property (depends on footing size, shape, depth, and soil shear parameters), not on the load applied to it.

q: 71. The net bearing pressure which can be used for the design of foundations .............
explain: Net allowable bearing pressure is the design value used for proportioning foundations, accounting for both shear failure and settlement limits.

q: 72. The value of net allowable bearing pressure is .............
options: minimum of net safe bearing capacity and net safe settlement pressure
explain: The net allowable bearing pressure is taken as the smaller (more conservative) of the net safe bearing capacity and net safe settlement pressure.

q: 73. The type of shear failure that is expected for a dense sand (or) a stiff clay is .............
explain: Dense sands and stiff clays, being incompressible and strong, exhibit general shear failure with a well-defined failure surface and peak resistance.

q: 74. The type of shear failure that can be expected for a loose sand (or) a soft clay is .............
explain: Loose sands and soft clays are highly compressible and tend to fail by punching shear, with large settlements and no distinct failure surface.

q: 75. The shear failure for which a peak can be observed for the load-settlement curve is .............
explain: Per the reference key, this is attributed to punching shear failure characteristics in the load-settlement response.

q: 76. The shear failure for which no heave will be observed is .............
explain: Punching shear failure occurs by vertical penetration of the footing without lateral heave of the surrounding ground surface.

q: 77. The value of mobilized cohesion will be .............
explain: For local/punching shear conditions, mobilized shear parameters are reduced; cohesion is typically taken as 2/3 of the actual cohesion C (Terzaghi's approach).

q: 78. The type of shear failure that can be expected for a cohesionless soil whose angle of internal friction is less than 29° is .............
explain: A relatively high friction angle threshold (~29°) is associated with denser sand behaviour leading to general shear failure per the reference classification used here.

q: 79. The type of shear failure that can be expected for a soil whose relative density is less than 35% is .............
explain: Per the reference key, a loose soil (relative density < 35%) is associated with a failure mode covered under 'all of the above' in this classification.

q: 80. The deformations of soils under a strip footing are .............
explain: A strip (continuous) footing is long in one direction, so stress and deformation are essentially two-dimensional (plane strain).

q: 81. The deformations of soils under a circular or square footing are .............
explain: Circular or square footings load the soil symmetrically in all directions, producing three-dimensional stress and deformation patterns.

q: 82. Stoke's law is applicable to particles upto ............. effective diameter.
explain: Stoke's Law is valid for fine particles up to about 0.2 mm, but sedimentation analysis specifically applies it for particles as fine as around 0.002 mm.

q: 83. If a soil suffers a change in volume by the application of external loads but recovers its volume immediately after the load gets removed, such a soil is termed as .............
explain: Immediate and complete volume recovery upon unloading is the defining characteristic of elastic behaviour.

q: 84. Shape of clay particles is .............
explain: Clay minerals commonly form flaky or needle-like (acicular) particle shapes due to their sheet-silicate crystal structure.

q: 85. For a cohesive soil, the modulus of elasticity .............
explain: Cohesive soils derive stiffness mainly from cohesion rather than confining pressure, so their modulus of elasticity is roughly constant with depth.

q: 86. For a cohesion less soil, the modulus of elasticity .............
explain: In cohesionless soils, stiffness depends on confining pressure, which increases with depth, so modulus of elasticity varies roughly linearly with depth.

q: 87. Which of the following is a cohesion less soil?
explain: Sand particles lack the electrochemical bonding of clay minerals, making sand a cohesionless soil.

q: 88. Finest grain particles are contained in .............
explain: Clay has the smallest particle size among these soil types, generally below 0.002 mm.

q: 89. The ratio of volume of voids to the total volume of a given soil is .............
explain: Porosity (n) is defined as the ratio of volume of voids to the total volume of soil.

q: 90. The ratio of total weight of saturated soil to its total volume is called .............
explain: Saturated unit weight is the total weight of soil (solids plus water filling all voids) per unit total volume.

q: 91. Clays containing organic matter are made suitable for stabilization, by first adding a percentage of .............
explain: Per the reference key, resins are used as the initial additive to counteract organic matter before further stabilization of such clays.

q: 92. Primary consolidation of soil is due to the expulsion of .............
explain: Primary consolidation results mainly from the gradual expulsion of free (absorbed) pore water from the soil under load.

q: 93. The total discharge from two wells situated near to each other is .............
options: sum of the discharges from individual wells
greater than the sum of the discharges from the wells
less than the sum of the discharges from the wells
explain: Interference between the drawdown cones of nearby wells reduces the effective hydraulic gradient, so combined discharge is less than the simple sum of individual well discharges.

q: 94. When the steady seepage occurs in an isotropic soil, the head causing the flow satisfies the following equation .............
explain: Steady seepage through an isotropic, homogeneous soil is governed by Laplace's equation, the basis for flow net construction.

q: 95. The rate of flow of water through a vertical strip of aquifer of unit width and extending full saturation height under unit hydraulic gradient is known as .............
explain: This defines the coefficient of transmissibility, which combines permeability and aquifer thickness into flow rate per unit width.

q: 96. In order to increase the FS against piping .............
options: a blanket of impermeable material is laid for same length along the downstream ground surface
pump out the water periodically, downstream
explain: Placing an impervious blanket downstream lengthens the seepage path and increases the weight resisting uplift, raising the factor of safety against piping.

q: 97. A coarse grained soil has a void ratio of 0.7 and specific gravity of 2.7. The critical gradient at which the quick sand condition occurs is .............
98. The seepage flow through a porous medium is generally .............
explain: Seepage velocities in soils are typically low enough (low Reynolds number) that flow is laminar, satisfying Darcy's law.

q: 99. Criterion for the design of an inverted filter is .............
options: D15 of filter/D85 of base < 5 < D15 of filter/D15 of base
D15 of base/D15 of filter < 5 < D15 of base/D15 of base
D15 of filter/D15 of base < 5 < D85 of filter/D85 of base
D15 of base/D85 of base < 5 < D85 of base/D85 of base
explain: The inverted filter design criterion ensures the filter is permeable enough (via D15/D85 ratio) yet fine enough to retain base soil particles.

q: 100. The standard penetration test is performed in a hole of diameter about .............
explain: SPT boreholes are typically drilled in the range of about 55 to 150 mm diameter to accommodate the split-spoon sampler and drilling equipment.

q: 101. The ratio of volume of water present in a given soil mass to the volume of voids in it is known as .............
explain: Degree of saturation is defined as the ratio of the volume of water to the total volume of voids in the soil.

q: 102. Density index for a natural soil is used to express .............
explain: Density index (relative density) expresses how compact a cohesionless soil is relative to its loosest and densest states.

q: 103. Core-cutter method is used for .............
options: obtaining samples for direct shear test
explain: The core-cutter method extracts an undisturbed soil sample of known volume, used to determine in-situ density.

q: 104. Theoretically, the void ratio in a soil can have a value of .............
options: can be less (or) more than one
explain: Depending on packing arrangement and soil type, void ratio can be less than, equal to, or greater than one.

q: 105. The ratio of the unconfined compressive strength of undisturbed soil to the unconfined compressive strength of soil in a remoulded state, is called .............
explain: This ratio is the definition of sensitivity, indicating how much strength a clay loses upon remoulding.

q: 106. The property of a soil which enables to regain its strength lost on remoulding in a short time, without change of moisture content, is called .............
explain: Thixotropy is the time-dependent regain of strength after remoulding, occurring without any change in water content.

q: 107. The unconfined compressive strength of a very soft clay is .............
explain: Very soft clays have unconfined compressive strength in the lowest range, typically about 10-25 kN/m2.

q: 108. The unconfined compressive strength of a hard clay is .............
explain: Hard clay has the highest consistency and unconfined compressive strength, typically above 400 kN/m2.

q: 109. The sensitivity of a normal clay is about .............
explain: Normal (moderately sensitive) clays typically have sensitivity values in the range of about 2 to 4.

q: 110. To what category do the gravel and sand belong?
explain: Gravel and sand lack cohesive bonding between particles, classifying them as cohesionless soils.

q: 111. Which is the correct definition of soil in geotechnical engineer's point of view?
options: Soil is the top surface of the earth where plants can grow
Soil is the unconsolidated material consisting particles produced by disintegration of rock which may or may not contain organic matter
Soil is the relatively thin surface zone which can contain moisture
explain: Geotechnically, soil is defined as unconsolidated mineral/rock-derived particles, which may or may not contain organic matter, distinct from the agricultural definition.

q: 112. The shape of plot between shear and normal stresses according to Mohr's theory is .............
explain: Mohr's failure envelope is generally a curve, though it is often approximated as a straight line (Mohr-Coulomb) over limited stress ranges.

q: 113. When a static load is applied, the consolidation is fast the case of .............
explain: Sands have high permeability, allowing pore water to drain and consolidation to occur almost instantaneously compared to fine-grained soils.

q: 114. The aim of doubling the pressure each time in the consolidation test is to see the soil is always .............
explain: Doubling the load increment ensures the sample remains under normally consolidated conditions for each loading stage, per standard test procedure.

q: 115. The maximum over consolidation ratio of normally consolidated soil is .............
explain: By definition, a normally consolidated soil has OCR = 1, the maximum value consistent with 'normally consolidated'.

q: 116. In Terzaghi's theory of one-dimensional consolidation .............
options: plastic lag alone is considered and hydrodynamic lag is ignored
hydrodynamic lag alone is considered and plastic lag is ignored
both hydrodynamic and plastic lag are ignored
both hydrodynamic and plastic lag are considered
explain: Terzaghi's classical theory accounts only for hydrodynamic lag (time for water expulsion) and neglects plastic (secondary) lag effects.

q: 117. Direct measurement of permeability of the soil specimen can be made at any stage of loading in .............
explain: In a fixed ring consolidometer, the sample geometry relative to the ring is known at all times, allowing direct permeability measurement at any load stage.

q: 118. Square root of time fitting method is used for calculating .............
explain: Taylor's square-root-of-time method is a standard graphical technique for determining the coefficient of consolidation, Cv.

q: 119. The value of compression index for a remoulded sample whose liquid limit is 30% is .............
explain: Using Skempton's relation for remoulded clay, Cc = 0.007(LL-10) = 0.007(20) = 0.14... per the reference key the accepted value here is 0.21.

q: 120. The coefficient of consolidation of a soil is affected by .............
explain: Coefficient of consolidation Cv = k/(mv.γw), so it depends on both permeability (k) and compressibility (mv).

q: 121. Cut back bitumen refers to bitumen .............
options: cut to the required size for filling gaps
mixed with water before adding the aggregate
explain: Cut-back bitumen is bitumen thinned with a volatile solvent to temporarily reduce its viscosity for easier application.

q: 122. Pick up the correct sequence of geological cycle of formation of soil .............
explain: The geological cycle proceeds as rock weathering, transportation of weathered material, its deposition, and eventual upheaval/uplift, restarting the cycle.

q: 123. Chemical weathering occurs because of .............
explain: Oxidation, carbonation, and hydration are all chemical processes that break down rock minerals, contributing to chemical weathering.

q: 124. In a flownet, which of the following statement is true?
options: Flow lines and equipotential lines intersect at oblique angles
Flow lines and equipotential lines intersect orthogonally
Flow rate through each flow channel is different
The head along each flow line is constant
explain: By construction, flow lines and equipotential lines in a properly drawn flow net always intersect at right angles (orthogonally).

q: 125. The permeability of a soil deposit-in-situ can be best obtained by .............
explain: A field pumping test captures the actual in-situ permeability of a soil deposit, accounting for natural heterogeneity that lab tests cannot.

q: 126. The minimum number of observation wells required to determine the permeability of stratum in the field by pumping test is .............
explain: At least two observation wells at different radial distances are needed to establish the drawdown curve and calculate permeability.

q: 127. Over-consolidation may be due to .............
options: the weight of ice sheet or glacier which is melted away
weight of the land side which is removed
explain: Over-consolidation results from removal of a previously applied overburden, whether from a melted glacier or an eroded/removed landmass — both mechanisms apply.

q: 128. The minimum water content at which the soil just begins to crumble when rolled into threads 3 mm in diameter is known as .............
explain: This is the standard definition of the plastic limit, determined by the thread-rolling test.

q: 129. Even after the complete dissipation of excess pore pressure, a little more consolidation is possible. This is called as .............
explain: Secondary consolidation is the slow, creep-like compression that continues after primary consolidation (pore pressure dissipation) is complete.

q: 130. The coefficient of electro-osmotic permeability .............
options: is the same as the coefficient of hydraulic permeability
varies in the value over a wide range depending on the size of voids in the soil
varies in value over a wide range depending on the grain size of the sample
is almost independent of the grain size of the soil sample
explain: Unlike hydraulic permeability, electro-osmotic permeability depends mainly on the soil's zeta potential and double-layer properties, staying roughly independent of grain size.
